utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in the courtroom and those outside the courtroom assisting us. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-84-T, the Prosecutor versus Ramush Haradinaj et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Emmerson you'd like to address the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Just very briefly on a scheduling issue. Your Honour will recall that yesterday the schedule for this week was agreed in relation to the recall of Witness 55 and certainly that had been my information throughout the whole of the week, that Witness 55 would be returning Thursday and indeed I planned to spend today finalising cross-examination preparation in relation to him after we finished in court. I understand that VWS have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps I can explain to you what happened. Arrival of the witness to be recalled would be only Thursday morning, which would most likely cause a delay in the start of that witness and as a keen interest in allowing this witness to return on Thursday so therefore the Chamber has considered whether we could afford to start late and then the only solution was to have the witness to arrive the day before, which would open the possibility to start cross-examination with him as well, if there would be any time remaining which of course we do not know yet but at least we would not lose time Thursday morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can I indicate --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I only learned of this possibility on walking into court a few moments ago and we are reasonably confident that there will be insufficient evidence today to use up the whole of the day in court, but I'm not in a position to begin cross-examination of Witness 55 until tomorrow morning because that has been the basis upon which I'd understood all week that the scheduling would occur and indeed that's the way I planned my preparation. On the other hand, I can give the Trial Chamber this guarantee, that cross-examination of Witness 55 if it starts promptly tomorrow morning at 9.00 will conclude well within the session and sufficient to allow re-examination to occur.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I do understand your problems. We'll discuss it. Let's first see how much time we need today because it might be a non-issue. We do not know yet how much time the witness to be called now will take and then we'll further discuss that. At the same time, if there are sometimes, I'm not saying always, but sometimes there are tiny separated issues which you could perhaps deal with, and I'm asking you to consider -- and also other counsel, to consider whether there are such issues which might not be part of a long line of questioning but separate issues which could be dealt with in --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm afraid to say in effect that because of the scheduling indications that I've had, I simply haven't been in a position to sit down and plan cross-examination in the way that Your Honour is indicating, in other words to identify separate issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. It's clear communication also from the Chamber has not been as it should be, that is something for the Chamber to consider, that communication will be better in the future. Then, Mr. Di Fazio, are you ready to call your next witness? MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, I am indeed. I call Milutin Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Visnjic. Before you give evidence in -- yes. Can you hear me in a language you understand, Mr. Visnjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Before you give evidence in this Court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require to you make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. The text is now handed out to you and I would like to invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please be seated, Mr. Visnjic. Mr. Visnjic, I see that you're taking some documents out of an envelope. May I instruct you that you should not consult any paper unless you have asked permission to do so. Mr. Visnjic, you'll first be examined by Mr. Di Fazio, counsel for the Prosecution. Mr. Di Fazio, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, before we begin, can we be assured that whatever documents Mr. Visnjic has with him, he has shared with the Prosecution so that we are in the event that such documents are to be pulled out or if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If they are to be pulled out we will ask what they are and whether they are known to others as well. But for the time being--

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The reason I'm raising that at this point is considering the history of litigation concerning this particular testimony it may be of some import.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: In a nutshell, the answer is simple. Yesterday Mr. Visnjic provided me with his own brief curriculum vitae. That was translated and provided to the Defence. Other than that, no other documents were produced to me yesterday. Examination by Mr. Di Fazio:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic could you please confirm if these personal details are correct? Your full name is Milutin Visnjic, father's name is Luka. You were born on the 27th of January 1952 in Kosovo and you're a Serb by ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can the witness please be shown 65 ter 1970, which I hope is his curriculum vitae that I just referred to. Thank you. Mr. Visnjic, is that document that you're looking at some brief notes concerning your curriculum vitae that you prepared and produced to me yesterday? And is that your signature at the bottom?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I seek to tender those -- that CV, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have some difficulties in -- first of all, I see on my e-court screen I see the original. Do I not have in my e-court system -- MR. DI FAZIO: Translation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: We've got hard copies, but I thought we had English version as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now it's loaded. Now we are. Please proceed, Mr. -- MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, you set out what you did basically between 1978 and 1993 and I want to get some more details of your work and experience from the point 1993 when you started working at the Pristina SUP. In your CV there you say that you commenced working there in 1993 as a ballistics expert and that you then went on to become a manager of a group of experts. First question is when precisely in 1993 did you start working there, if you can recall?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VISNJIC
utterances.text: On the 13th of December 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you immediately commence working for the SUP as a ballistics expert or in the field of ballistics or did you do other work for the SUP as a preliminary?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VISNJIC
utterances.text: I started working in the field of ballistics right away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell the Trial Chamber what training, if any, you received in order to carry out those sorts of duties?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VISNJIC
utterances.text: There was in-house training held by a ballistics expert who had been sent from the Secretariat of Novi Sad. I worked with him there and was trained by him as we went along.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long did that training last?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VISNJIC
utterances.text: He spent some six months there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what form did the training take? Was it simple observation of him going about his work? Was there a formal component, lectures or anything like that? Could you please provide a little more detail of the form that the training took?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VISNJIC
utterances.text: The training took place on the job. There was no extra training. We worked on individual cases, and whatever we came across as we were trying to solve a case, we would be trained in that particular area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long did your -- I'm sorry, I think you said you spent six months doing that sort of training. Did you receive any sort of formal qualification after doing the six months training?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VISNJIC
utterances.text: There was no formal qualification. I was only given a decision assigning me to that particular post.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Following the training, were you able to carry out your own analyses in the field of ballistics?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VISNJIC
utterances.text: After that, I worked on my own. However, whenever I was uncertain of certain matters, there were other ballistics experts in the MUP who would assist me in matters that I was not able to deal with on my own.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, at this time, if there is going to be a self qualification of expert, I think we should understand the names of the people who he consulted with and their qualifications or at least some indication of what experience they have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think as a matter of fact that -- yes. While that might have been the next question by Mr. Di Fazio, what the qualifications were of those the witness consulted with but before we continue I would have another question. Mr. Di Fazio, in your questions you're talking about ballistics. I always understood ballistics to be the science that deals with the flight of projectiles, et cetera, where some also include the technical aspects of firearm identification by marks, et cetera. How is the word ballistics used? Because that seems not to be entirely clear. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. I'll clarify that with the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you heard what His Honour said. We have been using the term ballistics. Perhaps we should be -- you should provide a little more precision as to the precise nature of what your field was and whether or not you include the term -- whether or not your field of expertise, if you possess it, comes within the term -- within the meaning of ballistics.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VISNJIC
utterances.text: One could term it as an analysis of traces left on cartridge cases. Most of the job involving ballistics or rather 90 per cent of it deals with the traces to be found on cartridge cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And bullets or just cartridge cases?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Cartridge cases and projectiles, bullets and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Di Fazio. You are aware that Mr. Guy-Smith would like to know -- MR. DI FAZIO: That's an excellent suggestion from Mr. Guy-Smith and I'm grateful to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But before I get on to that, there is just one more thing. Does your field of study incorporate or refer to the methods of -- the functioning of firearms and how they operate on bullets?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VISNJIC
utterances.text: In the course of work, we did not have time for that because this is not an institute dealing with research. What we were mostly concerned with was whether the weapons concerned were in working order, in proper order, and whether they could fire or not. MR. DI FAZIO: Would Your Honours just give me a moment? I want to see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio I take it there is some confusion about your question. I wouldn't mind if you would move on because talking about the traces left requires a certain understanding of how a weapon functions, and I think the witness understood it as whether they were testing weapons on their functioning, whereas I understood your question to be more limited. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned earlier that in the course of your carrying out your duties you conferred or spoke to other ballistics experts. Can you tell us how that came about and why it came about? In the normal course of your duties, in the normal course of carrying out analyses, why and how would you confer with other -- others possessing expertise in your field?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VISNJIC
utterances.text: As I said, right at the outset, there was the ballistics expert I worked with. Since the Secretariat in Pristina did not have a ballistics expert, it had experts who had been seconded by other offices. As I arrived there in Pristina, I came upon a ballistics expert who had already been there. It was with him that I worked with matching projectiles, marks and traces to be found on projectiles and rounds. With him, I worked on comparisons and matching. For the rest, I worked on my own. If I happened to be unsure about some marks, I would go to the MUP in Belgrade, and I would go to my colleague who worked with the security institute who was quite experienced in the matter; and I would consult him and he would be the one to have the final say so to speak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And can you just tell us the name of the gentleman who you worked with in Pristina, the ballistics expert who was there when you arrived? That's if you can recall it. If you can't --

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VISNJIC
utterances.text: I only know that he had originally come from the Novi Sad Secretariat. Vlado Dopudja, Vladimir Dopudja.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And how often did you have to go to Belgrade to speak with other ballistics experts?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VISNJIC
utterances.text: In the beginning, I did not have occasion to do that. However, as the number of cases of assault against the police and citizens grew, a decision had been taken higher up that whatever I worked on, I don't know when this practice started, but at any rate, from that point on, whatever cartridge cases I examined ultimately I had to take the cases and my findings to my colleague in Belgrade for the final matching and conclusions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you just tell us -- we know that you started working in 1993. I'd like you to focus on the period of time between 1993 and the beginning of 1998. Did this practice of your conferring with colleagues start before 1998 and if so, can you give us some idea of how long before you started this practice of conferring with colleagues?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VISNJIC
utterances.text: What do you mean since when? Do you mean whether it started before 1990?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps I'll be -- make my question a little clearer. You've told us that you started working in 1993 at the Pristina SUP. You told us that as the number of cases of assault against police and citizens grew, that your examinations and findings were taken to a colleague in Belgrade. When did that practice start, taking your findings and examinations to a colleague in Belgrade, approximately, if you can tell us?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VISNJIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm really not sure. I wouldn't want to venture to state a year, but I believe the practice started in 1995, but please do not take this as 100 per cent sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At any rate, before 1998?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this practice, did it involve -- tell us precisely what it involved. Was it a question of you simply handing over your results or did it involve discussion with your colleagues?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VISNJIC
utterances.text: Once I did my job, compared the cases, and arrived at the conclusion as to the weapons the cases came from, let me explain this more closely. The unresolved cases of cartridges found at crime scenes were stored in the Pristina SUP. One of the most characteristic groups of cases was placed in collections of cartridge cases. Any new case that we had involving cartridge cases would entail matching these cases with the cases found also at the same crime scene and then we would also match them with the cases that had been found earlier on. That is to say the cases from these collections. Once I did my part of the job, that's to say compared the newly found cases one with another and with the cases that had been found earlier on, I would reach my conclusions and then take all of the cases involved and my -- to my colleague to Belgrade. I would not present him with my findings beforehand. Rather, I would only present him with the case, the problem, the cartridges, and at the end of that process, we would compare our findings and reach the conclusion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have reason to discuss your findings with your colleagues on these occasions, to --

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VISNJIC
utterances.text: After my colleague would finish his work and make conclusions and we would discuss the work and all other things as well as future cooperation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Thinking back to the period between 1993 and 1998, this may be difficult to answer but please do the best you can, can you give the Trial Chamber an idea of how many examinations you might have conducted?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VISNJIC
utterances.text: Well, a lot, really a lot. I couldn't put a figure to it because in addition to these cases, there were also cases where we knew the perpetrators, such as murderers or suicides and similar cases. So in addition to this kind of work, we also had our routine cases, routine work, and that's why it would be difficult for me to give you a number of cases. I had full records, and as I have told you earlier, all of those records disappeared during the bombing and the records contained precise information on all of the cases.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Did you in the course of your duties, prepare reports --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, could I ask? You said it's difficult to give an estimate. Was it in the tens, was it in the hundreds, was it in the thousands? Could you give us some indication of the number of this type of cases, that is comparing and matching cartridges over five years?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, let me say up to 100, when it comes just to these unresolved cases, dozens. We could say dozens.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That would mean once every two, three, four weeks, such a case would come to you? Is that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, on average, one could say so, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the course of carrying out your duties, and following on from these analyses that you conducted, did you produce reports for judicial proceedings?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not entirely sure of the legal procedures in the former Yugoslavia but did that involve you actually testifying or giving evidence before tribunals and courts?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've -- you say in your CV that you -- that you became a manager of a group of experts and chief of forensics. When did that take place?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VISNJIC
utterances.text: Well, after about two years of work, I think. Since we did not have the people for the job, I was given a decision appointing me head of the section but since we didn't have the necessary experts, the required experts, I still continued working as a ballistics expert. My boss was killed in the bombing and I took over his duties as well as head of forensics.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. So you presumably took over as head of forensics in 1999 but before that, you'd become chief -- sorry, the manager of the group of experts around 1995. Is that a correct understanding of your evidence?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VISNJIC
utterances.text: Well, something like that. I'm not quite sure, but I do have that decision appointing me. Had I known that it would be necessary here, then I would have brought it with me. It was sometime after two years. Could have been in 1995 or in 1996, that I started heading this group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in your CV, you also say that you completed an OSCE ballistics course. When did you do that?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VISNJIC
utterances.text: Well, that was later, when I started working in the municipal Secretariat of the Interior in Belgrade. I think it was in 2003 or 2004, more likely in 2003.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And you also say that you are enlisted in the register of permanent court experts for ballistics and identification of traces of weapons and tools. I just would prefer if you would explain that to the Trial Chamber. I would just like you to explain to the Trial Chamber what precisely that means, what is this register, where is it located, when did you enlist in it?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VISNJIC
utterances.text: Since I was an employee of the Secretariat of the Interior, and I had a decision appointing me as a ballistics expert, I was an institutional expert and there was no need for me to be registered as a court expert. Once I retired in 2006, I became registered as a court expert within the region -- district court.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Earlier in your testimony you said that you had produced reports that -- for judicial proceedings. I'm not entirely sure of the difference between an institutional expert and a court expert. During the time that you were an institutional expert, did you nonetheless provide reports for -- to be used in judicial proceedings?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Most of our work was for the purposes of trials, of court proceedings. All of our reports were done in writing and were sent to courts. Naturally, they were also used in intelligence work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I now want you to turn your attention to events in 1998. At that time -- I don't think this is in dispute -- you were working with the SUP in Pristina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Earlier in your evidence you referred to comparisons that you would conduct between material found by police at crime sites and with material -- and results, and other analyses that you had conducted of other materials found at different locations and conduct comparisons. Do you recall giving that evidence a while ago?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I said so, and I described the procedure. All of the casings found on the spot were put in the collection, and we always compared newly found cartridges with the ones existing in the collection that stemmed from unresolved cases.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. It's the collection that I'd like you to provide a little more detail about, please. Do you know when this collection was started in Kosovo and how big it was by -- approximately how big it was by September of 1998?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VISNJIC
utterances.text: Well, the collection was already in existence when I started working there, so it had been established prior to my arrival there, and I just continued using it in my work. In 1998, since different types of weapons were used in various events, I would say that there were between 150 and 250 cartridge cases in the collection.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who actually put in the information into the collection to indicate where a particular item had been found? Did you do that?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VISNJIC
utterances.text: I did all the work concerning that. When the cartridge cases were brought in from the site, I would first record where they had been found, how many, so we kept records of that nature. Then following that, I would establish from what weapons they were fired and then from each group, I would select one or two characteristic cartridge cases, and then I would mark them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now in the process of recording where they had been found, were you dependent on records produced to you by other police officers who had been at the crime site?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Cartridge cases would arrive to me with accompanying documents containing a brief description of the event, time, date and place. So all of the cartridge cases would arrive with this brief description of the event.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thanks. Are you familiar with the actual process involved in finding an item of evidence at a crime site and getting it to you for analysis? Do you know -- are you familiar with that process?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VISNJIC
utterances.text: In principle, I know how this needs to be done, but I don't know how it was done in particular cases, because it was done by technicians who conducted on-site investigations. Those who investigated on the site, they would collect cartridge cases put them in bags, mark them with numbers, assigned on the spot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you recall what other information was required to be placed on these bags, if any, other than -- well, let me withdraw that question and rephrase it. Can you tell us precisely what information was required to go on to these bags from the point of collection?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VISNJIC
utterances.text: Well, I mostly received bags with the marked numbers. I did not receive complete report of the investigation conducted on site. I would just receive a brief description of the event and then brief information concerning the cases. All traces are normally marked with a number when an on-site investigation is conducted. So whenever a case is found, it is put in a bag and assigned a number, and this report would be sent to the relevant Secretariat. I myself would only receive a brief summary accompanying these cases so that in compiling my report, I could say, case number such and such was fired from such and such weapon and so on. So I had to know just the basics concerning the numbers so that I could include this in my report when describing particular groups of cases.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thanks. Do you know who prepared these sorts of summaries? Was it the seizing officer, the gentleman who actually found the item, or someone else?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VISNJIC
utterances.text: The procedure was such that the person going on site to conduct an investigation was duty-bound to write this technical report and then prepare a request that was sent to me. So a supervisor or head of the department would look at the request, review it, and then approve it to be sent to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thanks. Now, it's not in dispute here that the forensic department was hit by a NATO missile and records -- and -- records were destroyed. Firstly, you used to keep personal notes. They were destroyed in the -- when this missile struck the --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I would request that Mr. Di Fazio does not lead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio you're invited not to lead on this. MR. DI FAZIO: I'm happy to deal with it without leading. I didn't think it was in dispute.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Anything happen to the Pristina forensic department in 1999?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes. During the bombing, the entire forensics department was hit and it burned down, including my lab, my office, containing all the cartridge cases found on various sites, including the records that I kept.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thanks. Does that include your personal notes?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, including my personal notes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does it -- did it include the summary that you were just earlier referring to, the brief summary that accompanied the cases that came to you?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes. All of it. All of the replies that I wrote, all of my reports that were sent to various Secretariats of the Interior were sent out as originals and copies remained in my office, and all of them were destroyed in the fire that ensued.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thanks. I'd like to take you to a specific examination, please. MR. DI FAZIO: Can the witness be shown P445? I'd ask that he be shown the B/C/S version, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just have a look at that document and familiarise yourself with it, please.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First question is are you familiar with that sort of -- that sort of request for investigation -- for an analysis?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VISNJIC
utterances.text: Well, as I have said just now, each request that I received contained a brief summary of the event and the number of cartridge cases. Those were the typical records that I received, the documentation that I received. I apologise. Let me add something. In addition to the description of the event, the number of cartridge cases, the request must also contain the specific request, what they actually wanted me to do. So those three things were required, a brief description of the event, the cartridge cases found on the spot, and the request as to what needed to be done in relation to these cases.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in this particular case, Milan Stanojevic asked you to compare the various pieces of evidence with the archival material that you've referred to earlier in your evidence?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thanks. MR. DI FAZIO: Can the witness now be shown 65 ter 990? Again the B/C/S version, please. It's page 2, I'm told, that -- the actual report itself that I'm interested in. And can we go down to the bottom?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise that document?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is it?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VISNJIC
utterances.text: Well, this is my reply to the request that I received from the Djakovica Secretariat about the cases that were sent to me, accompanied by their request.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. That -- do I understand you correctly, this is your report that you produced in response to the earlier document that I showed you, P445?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's your signature at the bottom?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: May I ask what name that is at the bottom? MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, I'll ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that your name that appears at the bottom of the document?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, my name, first name and last name. MR. DI FAZIO: I think English translations are available, Your Honours. I think they should be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know what caused the question but I see on the line just above the signature, I see some five words, the last two apparently being Milutin Visnjic. I do not see any translation of the first -- the first ten letters. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps you find that out. MR. DI FAZIO: I will, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's not spend time on it in court. It could be something, please proceed. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may explain something, this is my title, what, the text before my name is my title, and that I am -- have a degree in mechanical engineering. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just read it out so the interpreters can translate it for the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VISNJIC
utterances.text: In front of my name is my title and it says that I have a bachelor's degree in mechanical engineering.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can the witness now be shown 65 ter 990, page 1, please? Again, if we could just go to the bottom of the document? Have a look at that document. Who is it -- who is it signed by, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VISNJIC
utterances.text: This was signed by my superior, head of the section, Radojica Kovac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why did he involve himself in forwarding the ballistics expert report?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VISNJIC
utterances.text: Every report produced by me or by my colleagues, when it was sent to the Secretariat of the Interior or to a court, had to have a cover letter accompanying it, and in that cover letter, it would be made clear that my boss had approved this report and that that was the meaning of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And now I apologise for switching around but can we now go back to your actual report, which is 65 ter 990, page 2? And -- thank you. It's the opinion that I'm interested in, which is the last paragraph in the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, I think that the two documents shown to the witness at least should receive an MFI number. Mr. Registrar. First, I think we are talking about the -- did you show the 21st of September 1st or you're using 65 ter numbers. MR. DI FAZIO: I think -- we've got, 21st of September document has already got an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's 445. And the other one it's the ballistics expert report and the accompanying cover letter. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. I'd be happy for them to be exhibited, to be marked as one, if Your Honours prefer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I would not mind to. In the electronic system it's one document at this moment, two pages, cover letter first and then report. MR. DI FAZIO: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar that would be number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours that would be P916.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. MR. DI FAZIO: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we can go to the opinion, please? You say that of the forwarded cartridges, firstly are you referring to the cartridges that were sent to you on the 21st of September 1998 by that gentleman Milan Stanojevic?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is stated in the first sentence of my report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And the -- yes, thanks. So it is. I apologise. Well, let me then ask you this directly, the one matter I'm interested in and that's this: You say that of the 14 -- of the forwarded cartridges, 14 are identical to 29 found in a certain place on 7th of March, Pljancor and 29 cartridges found on the 24th of March in a place called Gramocelj. When you say they are identical, when you say they are identical, what precisely do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VISNJIC
utterances.text: By identical, I mean the traces found on the cartridge cases are identical to the traces found on the cartridge cases recovered from Pljancor and Gramocelj. Let me explain what the traces mean. Automatic and semi-automatic weaponry leaves three or several characteristic traces on the cartridge case, one is the firing pin marks, the other one is ejector marks, the third mark is the breech face mark. The above-mentioned traces are the ones that can be found at the bottom of the cartridge case. There is also the fourth mark, which is the extractor mark, which is found on the edge of the cartridge cases. These are the four marks or traces that every automatic or semi-automatic weapon would leave on the cartridge case. On the basis of the marks that are compared one with another, one draws the conclusion as to whether the given cartridge case is identical to another such case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And if it is identical, what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VISNJIC
utterances.text: If the traces or marks are identical, this means that the cartridge cases examined were fired from the same weapon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, I seek to tender the expert report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I take it that that -- that the Defence would like to make submissions on the admission of the expert report.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Might we consider that position at the end of the witness's testimony?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Same for you, Mr. Guy-Smith?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And Mr. Troop?

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we will delay a decision. Yes. If I further questions? MR. DI FAZIO: I do apologise. I have no further questions. Thank you, Mr. Visnjic. I'm reminded if Your Honours please that the CV that I referred to earlier has not been given an exhibit number and it should be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, the CV of Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P917, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before the Chamber gives an opportunity to Defence counsel to cross-examine you, Mr. Visnjic, I'd like to have a look together with you to the 21st of September request for an examination. Could that be shown on the screen? Yes, could it be enlarged so that the -- one can read it? Yes. I'd like to do some simple calculations, if you wouldn't mind. Could you please follow me? I see that there are under label R-1, there are 40 cartridges. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Under R-2, there are 36. Under R-3, there are 16. Under R 4, there are four. Would you still agree with me?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Under R-5 -- R-5, there are five pieces, five cartridges. Under R-6, there are three, yes? That brings me to a total--

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of 104. If you would like to check that, perhaps someone writes it down and see whether we all agree on the simple -- MR. DI FAZIO: It's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's correct. Then we have another series that is RE 1. That's one piece. Re-2 is again one piece. That makes two, and altogether, 106. Now we have another series, that is D-1, six pieces. D-2, five pieces. D-3, again, five pieces, and D-4, one piece. This third series is a total of 17, which brings me to a total of 123 cartridges. Now, could I draw your attention to the 2nd of December 1998 report? Could that be shown on the screen please, that is P916. Second page, please. There, in the second line, it is said that 117 cartridges of a certain calibre were sent, one of another calibre, five of a 9 millimetre calibre, and one 7.9 millimetre calibre. If I add all this, I come to 124. Could you explain how you can, at the one hand, receive 123 cartridges and then in your comparison talk about 124? That puzzled me when I read these reports in their context.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VISNJIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Most likely there was an error in summing, 117 plus five is 122, and then there is another one and that's 123. So I apologise. The sum is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I am a layman in this respect. I see first 117, and now we go into detail, 7.62 times 39, one 6.-- 7.62 times 25, five 9 millimetre, and another one now 7.9 millimetre calibre. So I have 117 plus one plus five plus one makes 124, as far as my expertise goes in this field.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's correct. 124.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you resolve this puzzle for me, how you can receive 123 cartridges and how you can compare 124?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VISNJIC
utterances.text: I really don't know how it is possible that the report states a number that was wrong. I have to say that I referred to the cartridge cases that I examined. There must have been an error in the request that was submitted to me. I must admit that it is an error on my part not to have noticed that the number of cartridge cases is not the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Where the error lies, that's exactly the question that I was putting to you, but you have no clear recollection that you said one other cartridge slipped in or it did not -- we already noted that in the letter in which they sent the material to us, this was a mistake. You have no recollection, or do you have any recollection? But it seems that you're surprised by it now so I'm therefore not too optimistic to receive a clear answer from you.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VISNJIC
utterances.text: As I say, I don't recall where the error was made, but I do claim that the number of cartridge cases I wrote in my report is correct, because I could not have referred to cartridge cases that I did not examine. There were a great many such cases involving many cartridge cases. We were supposed to work under great time pressure, and I suppose that the lads who were working at scenes were also required to work at great speed, all of which could have led to some errors having been made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course, we have to consider all possible errors, one of them being that the cartridges you examined was not exactly the same sample as that was sent to you.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VISNJIC
utterances.text: No. The cartridge samples that I received, I just explained to you a moment ago, the procedure under which I worked. All the cartridge cases that were received from Djakovica, I said that first -- the first thing that I would do would be sort the cartridges out according to their calibre. Next I would sort them out according to the number of weapons. In this instant report, we don't have that, but normally we would have the number of cartridges coming from a given number of weapons and then the third section of the report would contain the comparisons or matching of these particular cartridges with the cartridges from the collections. I would say that the correct number of cartridges is the one contained in my report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then one more question about matches. You say 14 of the cartridges matched with 29 cartridges found on site on the 7th of March and with 29 cartridges found on site on the 24th of March. Do you remember these matches, were all these cartridges fired from one weapon or were there matches involving several weapons? Do you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VISNJIC
utterances.text: I think I do. The 14 cartridges out of the 117 cartridges of the 7.62 and 39 millimetre calibre were fired from the same weapon as the 29 cartridges that were found in the Pljancor village on the 7th of March 1998, and as the 29 cartridges found in the Gramocelj village on 24th of March 1998. Therefore, the 72 cartridges, as far as I was able to sum them up, were fired from the same weapon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. There were not more weapons involved, for example that the sample of 14 existed of ten from one weapon, four from another weapon, where the four matched with -- well, let's say 15 of the 29 and 13 of the other series of 29. It was just all one weapon. So when you described the matches here, there is only one weapon involved and not two or three or -- which would still be 14 matching with 29 and with 29. Do you understand what I mean, my question?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. The 14 cartridges and the two groups of 29 cartridges each were fired from one and the same weapon. Presumably, on the 7th of March, in Pljancor, there were several weapons, because as far as I recall, these cases of crime scenes, they always involved several weapons. So the 29 cartridges, the two groups of 29 cartridges, which were just a selection of probably many more cartridges that were found on the crime scenes were, together with the 14 cartridges that were found elsewhere, fired from one and the same weapon. So it means out of the 117 cartridges that were forwarded to me for examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That is clear to me. Mr. Di Fazio? MR. DI FAZIO: Could I just ask one or two questions following on from what Your Honours just asked?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I would not mind, although I always wait until all the questions by the Prosecution are put to the witness and -- but please do so. And then we might have a break and then after the break. MR. DI FAZIO: It only concerns one particular topic and that's the -- I'll ask the witness. Examination by Mr. Di Fazio: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've told us in some detail about the procedures that you adopted. When the samples came to you for analysis from, on the 21st of September, they were presumably analysed between that date and December, early December, early December. So for about two and a bit months, it's that two and a bit months that I'm interested in. During that time, who-- where precisely were the samples kept as they were being analysed?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VISNJIC
utterances.text: All the samples were kept with me, both the ones from earlier cases and the recent ones. All the samples stemming from unresolved cases were kept in my collection in my office.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the --

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VISNJIC
utterances.text: In order to be efficient, the traces were not sent back to the Secretariats that had forwarded these cartridges to me. They were all kept in my office to save time so that I can match them and compare them with the new ones that I receive rather than have to have to go back to the Secretariats to ask them to re-send them to me. That was why I kept all the cartridge cases from unresolved cases.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thanks. From the points of time that you received the cartridges or sorry, the bits of evidence for analysis, who was the official custodian of those pieces of evidence?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VISNJIC
utterances.text: We did not have special custodian. The cartridges were kept in a special safe that was located in my office.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And can you tell the Trial Chamber if -- what procedures, if any, existed to avoid any samples being mixed?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VISNJIC
utterances.text: All the pieces of evidence from a given scene were kept in a special bag labelled with the date and place, including the reference number of the request sent by the Secretariat. All of this was kept in one bag.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VISNJIC
utterances.text: Each and every evidence bag contained the basic information which told me immediately what the cartridge cases contained therein referred to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I suggest that we have a break now and that cross-examination -- Mr. Emmerson?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Cross-examination is not going to take very long, as far as I'm concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it more than five minutes because that will be the time to the break usually.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Maybe not but I'm very happy to take the break at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have a break and we'll resume at ten minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, you'll now be cross-examined first by Mr. Emmerson, counsel for the -- for Mr. Haradinaj. Please proceed, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, I've just got some general questions for you about the methodology involved in comparing cartridge cases. You told us in your evidence that there were four indicia, four signs that one looks for in a cartridge case for the purposes of comparison, pin markings, ejector markings, breech face markings, and extractor markings, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And obviously every weapon within a particular class will make markings in each of those four categories; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And your job, when making the comparison, is to determine whether the markings that you are looking at, say, for example, the extractor marks, whether these are what are described as class markings or individual markings characteristic of an individual gun; is that correct? You have to make that distinction.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VISNJIC
utterances.text: Well, these are the markings characteristic of a particular weapon. We compare cartridge cases to other cartridge cases in relation to a specific weapon, not a class of weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I understand that but when you identify a marking on a cartridge case, you have to make a decision about whether the marking that you're looking at is an individual marking made by a particular weapon or a marking made by a class of weapons or a marking that could be common to more than one weapon within its class? You have to make that judgement, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VISNJIC
utterances.text: Well, it is very difficult to establish the class of weapons because there are some weapons that leave a similar marking so in the initial stages, it is very difficult to say that it was the same type of weapons. This is why we compare directly the -- this with the already-existing markings.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I understand that. And then you have to decide whether, in your opinion, the particular marking you're comparing is one that could have been made by a number of different weapons or must have been made by an individual weapon. You have to make that assessment?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes. We make an assessment. It is generally known that every weapon has a particular, specific identity or an individual trace. The more a weapon is used, these individual features become much clearer because they are intensified after the weapon has been used for sometime.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Understood. So, for example, with some weapons, it's going to be much clearer to you that what you're looking at is two markings definitely made by the same weapon but with other weapons it might not be quite so clear; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is why there are so many of those traces. Out of those four markings that I explained, not necessarily all four are left. In some cases there are only two left or in some cases only three markings are left. If one of them is very -- is barely visible, then such traces, such markings or such cartridge cases are not taken into account when making an opinion. It is only in those cases where markings are completely identical that we take them into consideration. In cases when we are not sure, we disregard them.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And you would record, in the notes that you made at the time, the reasons that had led you to a particular conclusion, would you?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VISNJIC
utterances.text: What do you have in mind? Which trace? I didn't quite understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: With your working notes and the records that you kept at the time, the working notes as you're conducting an examination, you would record what the markings were that led you to the conclusions that you reached?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VISNJIC
utterances.text: Out of the group of cartridges, we would group them based on a calibre. Then within the same calibre, we would see how many weapons, and then we would describe the markings based on which we concluded that they were identical but that was not included in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No. I understand that but it would have been included in your working notes, your own personal working notes that were destroyed? That's where you would have recorded that type of information; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VISNJIC
utterances.text: No. I didn't record this type of information. In my personal notes or notebooks, I don't know how clear I was about it. But since we had a number of unresolved cases and we had a number of cartridges, in my report I would include -- or rather in my notes, I would write down relating to a particular event how many cartridges, what type of weapons and so on. And then I would write down whether these cartridges from the same group were identical to some other cartridges. That was the information included in my notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Did you record anywhere the workings that led you to a particular conclusion?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VISNJIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't do that. That was not a standard procedure when it came to our work.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Those are my questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Guy-Smith? Mr. Guy-Smith is counsel for Mr. Balaj and he'll now cross-examine you, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I want to understand one of the responses that you just gave, so I'm clear about what you were looking at. When you were doing your examinations, you recognise that there are a group of markings which are called class markings? I'm not talking about class of weapon but, rather, class characteristics that exist for all cartridges that would be-- that would go through a particular weapon, right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Maybe that's not exactly clear. What do you mean by saying a particular weapon?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask it in a different way.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the issue of examining cartridges, you're examining what are called tool marks which are marks that are made on the cartridge, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And you've identified four types of markings that you examined, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the kinds of markings that you examined, one type of marking is a marking which is a class characteristic, which is a marking that will be found as a result of it going through -- of a cartridge going through a particular type of weapon, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: There is another characteristic which is a subclass characteristic, and a subclass characteristic is present when there are those markings that arise out of the manufacturing process, which create a particular kind of anomaly in certain barrels but not in others, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And then there is this area that you called -- the last area which are individual markings, right?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VISNJIC
utterances.text: There are two types, individual markings and identificational traces. That's our terminology. Individual markings are the ones that you mentioned that pertain to the type of weapons. Whereas the identificational traces are the ones left by that specific weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: As I understand your testimony, when you were examining any cartridges, you did not memorialise, write down any notes, with regard to those distinctions between the class, the subclass, and the individual markings that you were examining, right?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harvey? Mr. Troop?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You were hidden.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Either way, we have no questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Di Fazio, let's first see whether --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps the Chamber first takes the opportunity to ask some questions. Judge Hoepfel has a question for you. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Please may I ask you how you establish these traces, one just by looking at it with your eye, two, with a magnifying glass, and three, with a microscope? You mentioned the microscope but is everything only done by microscopic analysis or how is your methodology?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VISNJIC
utterances.text: Since these are microtraces that cannot be seen with the naked eye, we used a comparative microscope or comparison microscope which is a specialist type of microscope specifically designed for this type of comparison. There are two plates on -- one for each cartridge, one from one group, one from another group. When we need to establish whether cartridges were fired from the same weapon or from different kinds of weapon, we put one cartridge on the left side of this comparison microscope and the other cartridge on the right side, on the right plate, and we make a comparison. As soon as we see that there is a match, then we appropriately group the cartridges. So from this entire group of cartridges that was forwarded to us, we first compare all of them to one randomly selected cartridge and then we select from that group all those cartridges that match the one that we had in our sample. As our sample. And then we continue, the process, randomly selecting cartridges from our collection to compare them to the ones that were forwarded to us. Once we see that there is a match, we appropriately group these cartridges that was the method of work we used with this comparison microscope when we needed to see whether there is a match. On this microscope, we can see the cartridge on the left and the cartridge on the right, and when making the comparison, if we establish that there is a full match, then we make appropriate conclusions and then proceed along the lines that I've just described.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: And may I ask you, you are speaking of "we." This is just your style of speaking or is it a group of people?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Or rather, I was referring to myself, since I was the sole ballistics expert, I was referring to myself. But this is just the standard procedure when working with the microscope.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I have a few questions for you as well. In using the comparison microscope, was there any camera fitted on it so that you could make a picture of what you saw under the microscope?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VISNJIC
utterances.text: Those were the older generation microscopes and unlike the new ones, they don't have a camera, they do not have the ability to make a picture. This is just plain visual comparison.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then were you asked some questions by Mr. Guy-Smith on characteristics, whether they were type of weapon characteristics, whether there were individual weapon characteristics. It was not entirely clear to me, since Mr. Guy-Smith seemed to have three categories in his mind and were you talking about two categories. I would like to further elaborate on that but before I do so, in your report, you write that in 14 of the forwarded cartridges and compared to the two series of 29 cartridges, you said they showed identical patterns of significant individual features. And for that reason, you come to the conclusion that these cartridges are identical, which I understand to mean that they are fired from the same weapon. Now, would you ever come to such a conclusion if not the individual characteristics of the weapon the cartridges were fired from would not be -- would not match? That is the -- would you come to such a conclusion ever on the basis of weapon type characteristics or only on the basis of specific, individual weapon characteristics?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VISNJIC
utterances.text: The conclusions can be made only when identification features are compared. Identification features pertain to a weapon. But as I said to you, each specific piece of weapon leaves a particular identification marking, has its own identification features. We can compare that to the papillary lines on fingertips, just as every person has their own fingerprint that is specific to that person, the same applies to weapons. Once we compare and match these features, and if we see that the match is full, then we make a conclusion that cartridges were fired from one and the same weapon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That would be such a conclusion would rest only on specific characteristics of the one weapon they were fired with; is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do you have any recollection of this comparison between the 14 and the -- 14 cartridge cases and the other cartridge cases you found in your collection? Do you have any fresh recollection, or is it just on the basis of paper that you say, "Well, this is what I did write down. This is what I always did. So --" I mean, or do you have any specific recollection of exactly this examination of these cartridges?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VISNJIC
utterances.text: I don't remember that specific examination. I remember the events in general. But the examination itself, and the procedure, no, I don't remember that in that particular case. I can just tell you what the general procedure is when making a comparison, but I don't remember that particular case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm asking this, for example, details such as these cartridges, were they delivered in a carton box sealed with tape or were they brought in a bag? I mean these kind of details of this specific examination. Do you have any recollection of that? If not, I would not be surprised after such a long period of time and also after -- well, having received many, many cartridges during your professional career, but I would not be surprised. I'm just asking if there is anything specific you would remember, we would like to hear, and if not, then of course, you couldn't say anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VISNJIC
utterances.text: I truly don't remember anything specific about that case. I don't remember what they were brought in. As a general rule, they were brought in bags, numbered and all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Di Fazio any need to re-examination the witness. MR. DI FAZIO: Just two very minor issues. Re-examination by Mr. Di Fazio:

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Both Defence counsel asked you about the keeping of notes. Was it necessary for you to conduct your examination and reach whatever conclusion you were going to reach in this particular case, and generally, to keep notes?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I object to the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. For asking for judgement or opinion rather than facts?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ask whether it was necessary, Mr. Di Fazio. That's-- MR. DI FAZIO: I'm not asking for a judgement. I'm just asking him about the normal day-to-day methods.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You can ask, were you able to make a conclusion or make -- draft a report without prior to that writing down your findings. Did you ever do that? Then we are talking about facts and about experience. MR. DI FAZIO: I'm happy to phrase it like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could you reach a conclusion without keeping notes?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VISNJIC
utterances.text: I could have reached a conclusion but it would have taken much longer, since there were quite a few such cases, in order to make it easier for me to work, I would keep notes of unresolved cases only. In my notebook, I had the description of the event, the number of cartridge cases, and the weapon from which it was discharged. All of this was labelled with numbers that I chose to facilitate my work. As I said, I had only one particular group of cartridge cases in my collection. In order to make sure that my conclusions were quite definite, I would take not only one cartridge from the collection I had that was characteristic. Rather, I took all those that I had in my collection in order to make my findings more conclusive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, let me try to understand. I think you can't make a report without making short notes. I mean, otherwise, you say 14 compared to 29. So there must be a piece of paper somewhere which says number 1 plus or number 1 minus match, no match, but do I understand that your notes did not include the details on which you concluded that there was a match? For example, pin mark unclear but the block mark perfect striae found. You didn't make those details in your notes. You would just write down match or no match on the basis of what you had seen? Is that the way you worked or --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. As I said, I only made notes of cartridge cases that were a match, and I would say, such and such a number of cartridges were fired from this one weapon and such and such a number of cartridges cases were fired from this other weapon. It was not standard procedure with us ballistics experts to write down that a match was found between different ejector marks and extractor marks. Rather, only when we found matches covering all these different markings examined would we write down that a match was found.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's clear. Mr. Di Fazio? MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You were asked by Mr. Guy-Smith whether you wrote down any notes concerning distinctions between features such as class, subclass and individual markings on the pieces of evidence that you examined. Was it necessary -- sorry. Why not? Why did you not keep such notes?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VISNJIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I did not fully understand your question. Can you please clarify it a bit?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sure. Mr. Guy-Smith one of the Defence counsel, asked you this: When you were examining any cartridges you did not memorialise or write down any notes with regard to those distinctions between the class, the subclass and individual markings that you were examining. And you said yes. Any reason why you did not make notes?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VISNJIC
utterances.text: I've just given my answer. It was not standard procedure to make notes indicated on the traces on the basis of which a match was found. Only when I reached a conclusion based on the existing markings that are normally used to identify a certain weapon, I would write down what my finding was without any additional reasons that led me to that conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I thank you. And just the last issue that I want to ask you about is one that you've just raised in your answer. You say it was not standard procedure. Can you tell the Trial Chamber where it was not standard procedure? Do you have any information as to whether or not at the time it was standard procedure -- not standard procedure in the former Yugoslavia or whether it was not standard procedure on a broader-- in a broader sense or simply not standard proceed in your department?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VISNJIC
utterances.text: This was not standard procedure. Since there were only three centers in Belgrade, Novi Sad and Pristina, I was in touch with all my colleagues who did the same job I did. The procedure applied was the one that I used. You remember that I told you that the first colleague I contacted was the ballistics expert from Novi Sad. Later on I had contacts with my colleagues in Belgrade. These were the centres I collaborated with, and they all used the method of work and note keeping that I used.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Re, if time would be given to you to conclude or to add something to examination-in-chief, I did not hear any objection to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness 55. I'm glad to see you back. You may have been surprised a little bit that we invited you to come one day earlier than it was scheduled at the time. The main reason is that we had some concern that if you would arrive in the morning, that we would most likely have a late start but I'd say not before 10.00 or 10.30 and since we cannot finish in the afternoon -- we cannot continue in the afternoon we were worried that you would not be able to go back to the place of your residence on that same day.
