Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, I do. But I have something to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is there something -- I suggest the following, that if you would like to say something, that first Mr. Re will -- that first you answer a few more questions and that you then get an opportunity to address the Chamber, or is it so urgent that you would like to address us now and then we also have to keep in mind on whether you would like to address us in private session or whether it could be public.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to address you, Your Honours, in private session, in order to explain a few things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll see to what extent, because usually witnesses are there to answer questions but we'll give you an opportunity to say something in private session. We have keep a close eye on the way you address us, whether that's appropriately done by a witness. We turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are in open session with the exception of the curtains being down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could the curtains be pulled up again. If I could have the assistance of those, although not trained for it. The Chamber would like to deal with a few procedural matters to use the time this morning. I will first read a decision and read the reasons for a decision in respect of Witness 64. I'll start with the first one. The decision on Prosecution's 20th motion for trial-related protective measures. The Prosecution's 20th motion for trial-related protective measures filed on the 13th of July 2007 with corrigenda filed on the 3rd of August and the 16th of August 2007, the Prosecution applied for protective measures for a person whose two witness statements have been admitted into evidence in accordance with Rule 92 bis through the Chamber's decision of the 11th of July 2007. The Prosecution asked for the assignment of a pseudonym and also that the witnesses referred to by this pseudonym in all public documents and that no identifying information of the witness is disclosed to the public. The Chamber notes that in principle, the trial must be open to the public. Protective measures, therefore, may only be granted if there is an objectively grounded risk to the security or welfare of the witness or the witness's family should it become known that the witness has given evidence before the Tribunal. The party seeking protective measures for a witness can satisfy this standard by showing that the threat was made against the witness or the witness's family, or by demonstrating a combination of the following three factors: 1, the witness's testimony may antagonise persons who reside in a specific territory; 2, the witness or his or her family live or work in the territory, have property in the territory or have concrete plans to return to live in the territory; and 3, there exists an unstable security situation in that territory which is particularly unfavourable to witnesses who appear before the Tribunal. The Chamber notes that no threats were made against the witness and therefore turns to examine whether the three above-mentioned conditions are met. The Chamber has accepted the parties' agreement that there exists an unstable security situation in Kosovo which is particularly unfavourable to witnesses who appear before the Tribunal. The witness and her family live in a town in Kosovo. Therefore the third and the second condition of the test are met. However, the Chamber is not satisfied that the first condition of the test is met. The witness stated that some day in July 1998, her husband disappeared and that in 2004, she was informed that his remains had been found. The witness stated that she does not know who killed her husband or why he disappeared. Since the witness's evidence does not point to any particular person, the Chamber fails to see how the content of the witness's testimony may antagonise people who reside in Kosovo. For these reasons, the Chamber denies the Prosecution's request for pseudonym and redaction of all identifying information. The witness's statements are currently under seal. Therefore, the Chamber orders the registrar to make the statements public, unless the Prosecution informs the Chamber by 5.00 p.m. On the 19th of September 2007 that it chooses to withdraw the evidence. This concludes the Trial Chamber's decision on the Prosecution's 20th motion for trial-related protective measures. I will now give the reasons for a decision on the Prosecution's motion for trial-related protective measures for Witness 64. The Trial Chamber would like to give its reasons for having granted the protection motion for trial-related -- the Prosecution's motion for trial-related protective measures for Witness 64. On the 29th of August 2007, the Prosecution applied for the trial-related protective measures of pseudonym and face and voice distortion for Witness 64. The Chamber notes that no threats have been made against Witness 64. The test for granting protective measures in the absence of threats has been set out by the Trial Chamber many times before, and need not to be reiterated here. The Chamber has accepted the parties' agreement that there exists an unstable security situation in Kosovo, which is particularly unfavourable to witnesses who appear before the Tribunal. Given the nature of the witness's testimony, the Chamber is also satisfied that it may antagonise persons who reside in Kosovo. Therefore, the first and the third conditions of the applicable test are met. Witness 64 and his family own property in Kosovo. Witness 64 has expressed fear that following his testimony before the Tribunal, he may never be able to return to Kosovo to live there or to sell his property in Kosovo. In court, Witness 64 explained that he would wish to live in Kosovo with his family should the conditions allow for their return. He also stated that his parents had a strong wish to return to their home in Kosovo and that if they would return, he would travel to Kosovo more often. Witness 64 further explained that if it turns out to be impossible for them to return to Kosovo, he and his family would like to be able to sell their property. I refer to the pages 7819 and 7825 of the transcript. The Chamber understands that the plans of Witness 64 and his close relatives to return to Kosovo or sell their property there depend to a large extent on future developments in Kosovo. The Chamber is satisfied that Witness 64, and his relatives, do, in effect, intend to return to Kosovo even if this plan is conditioned upon an improvement of the situation there. The Chamber does find that the requirements for granting protective measures were met and therefore granted the protective measures of pseudonym and face and voice distortion. This concludes the Chamber's reasons for the decision on protective measures for Witness 64.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Just before Your Honour continues I noticed from the transcript that both of the rulings that Your Honour has given are recorded as having been given in respect of Witness 64.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's wrong. In the beginning, I said reasons -- no, the decision on the 20th motion, and reasons for Witness 64. I then-- though I think I used the word Witness 64 again I moved to the other decision first.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm simply making that observation for the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's now clear on the transcript and the Chamber appreciates your comments, Mr. Emmerson. A few other matters. The Chamber has considered whether it would invite the Prosecution to read 92 ter statements. We have decided that it would not make that much sense at this moment. Why? Reading out 92 ter statements was meant to inform the public about the basis, the basic elements of the testimony of that witness so as to better understand any follow-up questions in relation to that statement. Now, a practice has developed, a practice the Chamber is not extremely happy with, that up until the last minute before the witness appears, that a battle is ongoing on what could and could not be dealt with under Rule 92 ter. That means that usually the final version to be admitted for the 92 ter statement is not yet available at the beginning of the testimony, let alone a summary of that 92 ter statement. The Chamber would urge the parties to already include in whatever negotiations there are in relation to admissible or non-admissible elements in 92 ter statements to already prepare a summary. Whereas the discussions on 92 ter statements often go into details, summaries very often could be prepared and might cause especially since there are no evidence, might cause less problems. We could then restore what we initially had in mind, that is to have a summary of the witness statement to be read so that the public understands what the testimony is about and then to put further questions to the witness. However, to read 92 ter statements days or weeks after the witness has given testimony could not serve this purpose any more. Therefore, the Chamber decided not to invite to read the 92 ter statements. Then we have a few matters in relation to the admission of exhibits.
